steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the "Data structures" section of a Wikipedia article on append-only storage: why data structures are made append-only, typical examples, hardware and software environments that force it, and the downside of unbounded growth.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Immutable objects -> append-only; benefits
- Log files and log-structured systems; blockchains
- Environments that mandate append-only (functional languages, flash, SMR drives)
- Growth over time and rewriting / garbage collection

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Immutable objects
  - many data structures and databases implement them -> effectively append-only
  - benefits: data consistency, performance, rollbacks
- Logs
  - log file = prototypical append-only data structure
  - log-structured file systems and databases similar: every change (transaction) logged; on retrieval program combines pieces found in log
  - blockchains add cryptography to logs -> every transaction verifiable
- Mandated by hardware/software environment
  - purely functional languages: all objects immutable, every function pure, no global state
  - flash: pages written ("programmed") once before erasing; erasing at "blocks" level (hundreds to thousands of pages) -> each block append-only set of pages
  - shingled magnetic recording hard drives: no random writes, writing a track clobbers neighboring (usually later) track -> each "zone" append-only
- Growth
  - more space for "stale" data only in history, more time parsing it
  - many systems implement rewriting (copying garbage collection): new structure with only current version, optionally a few older ones

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Many data structures and databases implement immutable objects, which in effect makes their data structures append-only. There are many benefits to implementing an append-only data structure, for example it ensures data consistency, it improves performance, and it permits rollbacks.

The log file is the prototypical append-only data structure. Log-structured data structures, which are found in log-structured file systems and databases, work in a similar way. Every change (transaction) that happens to the data gets logged by the program, and when the data is retrieved the program has to combine the pieces of data that are found in this log file. Blockchains add cryptography to the logs, so every transaction can be verified.

- append-only can also be mandated by the hardware or software environment:
  - purely functional languages: all objects immutable, every function pure, no global states
  - flash storage: pages written ("programmed") only once before erasing; erasing by "blocks" of hundreds to thousands of pages -> each block an append-only set of pages
  - shingled magnetic recording hard drives: can't write randomly, writing a track clobbers a neighboring, usually later, track -> each "zone" append-only
- growth: more space on "stale" data only in history, more time wasted parsing; rewriting (copying garbage collection) creates new structure with only current version and maybe a few older ones

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Many data structures and databases implement immutable objects, which in effect makes their data structures append-only. There are many benefits to implementing an append-only data structure, for example it ensures data consistency, it improves performance, and it permits rollbacks.

The log file is the prototypical append-only data structure. Log-structured data structures, which are found in log-structured file systems and databases, work in a similar way. Every change (transaction) that happens to the data gets logged by the program, and when the data is retrieved the program has to combine the pieces of data that are found in this log file. Blockchains add cryptography to the logs, so every transaction can be verified.

Sometimes the hardware or software environment also mandates append-only data structures:

In purely functional programming languages all objects are immutable, because every function is pure and there are no global states.

Flash storage pages can only be written to ("programmed") one time before they are erased. Erasing on a flash drive works at the level of "blocks", and these cover hundreds to thousands of pages, so each block is treated as an append-only set of pages.

Hard drives using shingled magnetic recording cannot be written randomly, because writing on one track would clobber a neighboring track, which is usually a later one. So each "zone" on the drive is append-only.

Append-only data structures grow over time. More and more space goes to "stale" data that is only found in the history, and more time is wasted parsing this data. A number of append-only systems implement rewriting (copying garbage collection), where a new structure gets created that only contains the current version and optionally a few older versions.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Many data structures and databases implement immutable objects, which effectively makes their data structures append-only. Implementing an append-only data structure has many benefits, such as ensuring data consistency, improving performance,[1] and permitting rollbacks.[2,3]

The prototypical append-only data structure is the log file. Log-structured data structures found in log-structured file systems and databases work in a similar way: every change (transaction) to the data is logged by the program, and on retrieval the program has to combine the pieces of data found in this log file.[4] Blockchains add cryptography to the logs so that every transaction can be verified.

Append-only data structures may also be mandated by the hardware or software environment:

In purely functional programming languages all objects are immutable, since every function is pure and global states do not exist.[5]

Flash storage pages can only be written to ("programmed") once before erasing. Erasing on a flash drive works at the level of "blocks", which cover hundreds to thousands of pages, so each block is treated as an append-only set of pages.[4,6]

Hard drives that use shingled magnetic recording cannot be written to randomly, because writing on a track would clobber a neighboring, usually later, track. As a result, each "zone" on the drive is append-only.[7,1]

Append-only data structures grow over time, with more and more space dedicated to "stale" data found only in the history and more time wasted parsing it. A number of append-only systems implement rewriting (copying garbage collection), so that a new structure is created containing only the current version and optionally a few older ones.[2,8]
